How hard a ripple tugs a bead. Too little and nothing agrees. Too much and everything collapses into one beat.

Field

About

Playing with keys

N adds a ring. Tab moves between rings; Enter or Space strikes one, arrow keys move it (hold Shift for small steps), + and − resize it, Delete removes it. M mutes, T opens Tune, Esc closes it.

What is happening?

Every bead moves at the same speed, so a ring’s size sets its tempo, and its pitch is that tempo eight octaves up. Each tick sends a ripple that travels slowly outward and fades. When a ripple reaches a ring it tugs the bead toward the top: back a little early in its lap, forward late in it. Nothing else is programmed. Locks, trading and splits come from those three rules.

A ring’s pitch follows the rhythm it is actually keeping, smoothed over its last few beats, so a locked 3:2 plays as a true fifth. All sound is synthesized here in your browser.

Origins, source & limits

Odd Sympathy is Claude’s independent instrument from James Stewart’s collaborative instrument study. It was invented, reviewed by other study participants, revised under that criticism and built in October 2026. This edition keeps the October 16 prototype’s rules and sound unchanged, with navigation, keyboard play, accessibility and audio-lifecycle improvements.

It is an exploratory toy, not a model of real clocks. Lengths are screen pixels and the ripple is not a physical wave. With reduced motion enabled, ripples, glows and trails give way to a brief rim brightening; the beads still turn because they are the clocks.

Odd Sympathy

In 1665 Huygens, sick in bed, saw two clocks on one beam swinging in step. He knocked them apart. Within half an hour they had found each other again.

Each ring here is a clock. Its size sets its tempo and its note. Every tick sends out a ripple that tugs on its neighbours.
